428.title: Bechukotai: still remembered (Leviticus 26:42–45)
428.hook: even after the warnings, God remembers the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham
428.howItsDone: When the warnings of Leviticus 26 are read in many synagogues, the reader's voice returns to full strength for the closing verses of remembrance; the theme of God remembering the covenant with the ancestors runs through Jewish prayer, especially on Rosh Hashanah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tochacha, the warnings read in a low voice. Your line was hard words, softly. Today, the end of that chapter.

There's a drawer in a lot of homes with old things nobody throws out: a hospital bracelet from a birth, a note in a grandparent's handwriting, a ring that doesn't fit anyone anymore. The things in that drawer have outlived the quarrels around them. A family can fight for years, and the drawer still holds the proof that someone once promised to love someone. The warnings in Leviticus twenty-six get very dark: an empty land, a scattered people. Then, right at the bottom, the chapter opens a drawer.
screen: `A DRAWER OF OLD PROMISES.` → `IT OUTLIVES THE QUARRELS.` → `AT THE BOTTOM, A DRAWER OPENS.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-two. After the exile, after the empty fields, God says: "then will I remember My covenant with Jacob, and also My covenant with Isaac, and also My covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land." Listen to the order. Not Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the way the names usually run. It goes backwards. Rashi offers a reading: it's as if God reaches back one generation at a time. Jacob alone would be reason enough; and if not, there's Isaac with him; and if not, Abraham. The memory keeps reaching further back until it finds enough. Verse forty-four says what remembering means in practice. Even when they're in the land of their enemies, God will not reject them, nor abhor them so as to destroy them utterly, and break the covenant. And verse forty-five adds one more memory: the covenant with the generation brought out of Egypt. Notice what the chapter doesn't do. It doesn't cancel the warnings or pretend they weren't said. The hard words stand. But the chapter closes on memory, a promise older than the failure, held by the one who made it. The relationship can be strained to breaking. Verse forty-four says it isn't broken.

segments.voice: Go back through the years slowly, the way the verse goes back through the generations, and find one promise once made to you: a parent who said I'll always come get you, a teacher who said you can do this, a friend who said call me, any hour. Remember the voice, the room, the moment. Notice that the promise still exists, even if the person is far away, or gone, or changed.
Bechukotai, Leviticus's last portion. After the blessings and the warnings, it ends with God remembering: the covenant, the ancestors, and the land.
Your line: still remembered. The warnings stand, and the promise is older. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

429.title: Leviticus close: chazak
429.hook: the book of holiness ends and the synagogue says chazak
429.howItsDone: When the last verse of each of the five books of the Torah is read in synagogue, the congregation calls out chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek, and the reader repeats it; Leviticus is finished each spring with Bechukotai.

segments.voice: Yesterday the warnings ended in memory. Your line was still remembered. Today, the last verse of Leviticus.

Leviticus doesn't end with a bang. Its last chapter reads almost like an appraiser's table. Someone has vowed the worth of a person to the sanctuary, and the Torah sets the amounts: so many shekels for an adult in the prime of life, less for a child, less for the old. Then a quiet mercy. If the one who vowed is too poor to pay, the priest sets the amount by what that person can afford. One more verse, and the third book is done. In the synagogue, that's the moment for three words, called out loud.
screen: `AN APPRAISER'S TABLE.` → `WHAT THE POOR CAN AFFORD.` → `THREE WORDS, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: After the vows and the gifts to the sanctuary comes the last verse: "These are the commandments, which the LORD commanded Moses for the children of Israel in mount Sinai." Mount Sinai, the same mountain Behar opened with: a bookend. Then comes the call that closed Exodus too: chazak, chazak, v'nitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us be strengthened, and the reader says it back. Think about what this book held. It opened with a call, Vayikra, and with offerings, korbanot, from a root that means to draw near. It walked through the priests' first day and a sudden grief. Skin and walls that needed healing, and a priest who went out to the person. Yom Kippur and the goat sent into the wilderness. Holiness spoken to everyone: corners of the field, no stumbling blocks, love your neighbor as yourself. Appointed times. Land that rests, liberty proclaimed, guests on God's earth. Blessings, warnings, and memory. Jewish children were once started on this book first. Plenty of adults find it the hardest. Either way, you've walked through it. And notice the plural at the end: let us be strengthened. No one finishes a book of the Torah alone.

430.title: In the wilderness
430.hook: the book's Hebrew name means "in the wilderness", where the Torah was given in no one's land
430.howItsDone: The portion Bamidbar is usually read on the Shabbat just before Shavuot, the festival of the giving of the Torah, and many teachers connect the two: the Torah was given in the wilderness, open to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday Leviticus closed and the room called chazak. Your line was be strong. Now a new book opens.

In English it's called Numbers, which sounds like a tax form. The title, handed down from old translations, names the book for its census counts. Fair enough: it opens with a headcount. But the Hebrew name comes from the first verse's fifth word, and it paints a different picture. Bamidbar. In the wilderness. Not a book of arithmetic. A book of sand, and stars, and a whole people sleeping in tents between the place they left and the place they haven't reached.
screen: `NUMBERS: A BOOK OF COUNTS?` → `BAMIDBAR: IN THE WILDERNESS.` → `BETWEEN LEAVING AND ARRIVING.`

segments.voice: The book begins: the LORD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai. The verse dates it to the second year after Egypt. The people have been camped at the mountain, and soon they'll set out. Nearly everything in this book happens out here, in the midbar, the open land with no cities and no owners. The rabbis asked a pointed question: why was the Torah given in a wilderness at all, and not in the land of Israel, or in a great city? A midrash called the Mekhilta answers: so that no one could claim it belonged only to them. It was given openly, in a place that belongs to no one, so anyone who wants it can come and take it. Another midrash, on this book, lists three things the Torah was given through: fire, water, and wilderness. What do they share? They're free. Nobody charges for a desert. Then the same tradition turns it inward. The Talmud says: a person who makes themselves like the wilderness, open, unclaimed, not full of themselves, receives the Torah as a gift. A crowded mind has no room. An empty place can hold a voice. So this stretch of the path is the wilderness book. Counting and camping, complaining and rebelling, scouts and prophets, a talking donkey and a long road. A generation that left slavery learning, slowly, how to be free. The first lesson is the place itself.

segments.voice: If you can, go to the emptiest spot nearby, a bare corner, a quiet stairwell, a window facing open sky; if you can't move, put the phone face down and clear one surface in front of you. Sit with the emptiness and notice how quickly the mind tries to fill it. Let it stay empty a little longer than is comfortable, like open ground waiting for a voice.
Bamidbar. In the wilderness: the Hebrew name of the book of Numbers, and of the open, ownerless place where the Torah was given.
Your line: the wilderness teaches. A new book, and a long road ahead. Day four hundred thirty.

431.title: Bamidbar: counted by name (Numbers 1:2)
431.hook: a census "by their polls", each person counted, not just a total
431.howItsDone: Jewish custom avoids counting people by number; to check for a minyan of ten, some recite a ten-word verse, one word per person, or count "not one, not two." The census of Numbers 1 is read each year in the portion Bamidbar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bamidbar, in the wilderness. Your line was the wilderness teaches. Today, the first thing the wilderness book does.

Six hundred three thousand, five hundred fifty. That's the total the book of Numbers gives for its first census: men twenty and older, ready to go out with the army. It's the kind of number that makes eyes glaze. A stadium, a city, a statistic. And yet the Torah's instructions for getting there are oddly personal. Not count the tents. Not estimate the crowd. Something slower, one person at a time. Before the wilderness journey even begins, God asks Moses to stop and count, and the way the count is described says more than the total.
screen: `603,550.` → `A STADIUM, A STATISTIC.` → `ONE PERSON AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Numbers, chapter one, verse two. Take the sum of the whole congregation, by families, by fathers' houses, "according to the number of names, every male, by their polls." Polls is old English for heads. The Hebrew is l'gulgelotam, by their skulls, head by head. And the number of names: each one counted as a someone, not a something. Rashi, at the very first verse, asks why this people gets counted so often: once leaving Egypt, once after the golden calf, and now again. His answer: because they're dear to God, God counts them often, the way someone counts a treasure, not to learn the total, but to touch each piece again. Other commentators, like Nachmanides, read the counting by name as a way of giving each person dignity: you didn't just pass through a gate, you stood before Moses and Aaron and said who you were. There's a flip side, and Jewish custom takes it seriously. The Talmud warns against counting Jews by number directly, and there's a story of King Saul counting his soldiers by pebbles or lambs instead. So when a congregation checks whether ten adults are present for a prayer quorum, the custom is not to say one, two, three. Some say a verse of ten Hebrew words, one word per person. Others count not one, not two. Both come from the same instinct. A person is never only a number. Count every head, and never reduce a head to a count.

segments.voice: Think through your week: the person at the front desk, the bus driver on your route, the neighbor two doors down, the new person at work you've been calling hey, you. Bamidbar, the wilderness book, which opens by counting a people one name at a time.
Your line: count every head. Every name belongs to a whole person. See you tomorrow.

432.title: Bamidbar: banners around the center (Numbers 2)
432.hook: each tribe camps under its own banner, all facing the sanctuary
432.howItsDone: The arrangement of the camp in Numbers 2 is read in the portion Bamidbar; some synagogues display the twelve tribal symbols, and teachers use the camp as a picture of a people that keeps its many identities around one shared center.

segments.voice: Yesterday the people were counted one name at a time. Your line was count every head. Now that everyone's counted: where does everyone go?

A wedding seating chart is a small war. The bride's cousins at one table, the groom's college friends at another, two great-aunts who must never sit together. Every table different, every table set around the same dance floor. Now take away the hall, put it in the desert, and make it twelve tribes, hundreds of thousands of people, setting up camp every time they stop. You'd expect a scramble. Numbers chapter two draws a map instead, and the shape of that map is the lesson.
screen: `EVERY TABLE, ONE DANCE FLOOR.` → `TWELVE TRIBES IN THE DESERT.` → `THE SHAPE IS THE LESSON.`

segments.voice: The instruction is simple. The children of Israel will camp each one by his own banner, with the signs of their fathers' houses, around the tent of meeting, at a distance. The Hebrew word for banner is degel. Twelve tribes form four camps of three. To the east, toward the sunrise, Judah leads, with Issachar and Zebulun. To the south, Reuben. To the west, Ephraim. To the north, Dan. Inside that ring, the Levites camp in a closer circle, and at the very center stands the Tabernacle. When they march, they march in that order, and when they stop, the same square forms again. The map does two things at once. First, everyone keeps their own banner. No tribe is told to blend in. Rashi, following the midrash, says each banner had its own color, matching that tribe's stone on the high priest's breastplate. Twelve colors, not one. Second, every banner is set around the same middle: they camp round about the tent of meeting, on every side of it. The differences are real, and they're arranged around something shared. A later midrash imagines the nations of the world looking at this camp with longing, not for its size, but for its order. It's an old picture of a people that is many and one at the same time. You don't have to stop being your tribe to be part of the whole. You just have to face the center.

segments.voice: Ask what your banner is, your family, your town, your background, your way of praying or not praying, and be glad of it for a moment. Then picture someone you live or work beside who flies a different one, and be glad of theirs, too. Last, ask what center you share with them: a street, a project, a child, a table.
Bamidbar, the wilderness book. Today it draws a map: twelve banners, four camps, and one center everyone faces.
Your line: everyone around the center. Twelve colors, one middle. Day four hundred thirty-two, done.

433.title: Bamidbar: set apart to serve (Numbers 3:12)
433.hook: the tribe of Levi is set apart to serve the sanctuary
433.howItsDone: In many synagogues a Levite is called second to the Torah reading, after a kohen, and Levites wash the hands of the kohanim before the priestly blessing. Some families with names like Levi, Levine or Halevi trace descent from the tribe.

segments.voice: Yesterday twelve banners circled one center. Your line was everyone around the center. Today, the ring closest to the middle.

In some synagogues, just before the priestly blessing, a few people slip out and come back with a pitcher and a basin. They pour water over the hands of the kohanim, the priests' descendants, who are about to bless the congregation. Then the kohanim go up front, and the pourers go back to their seats. No speech, no spotlight. Ask who they are, and you'll often hear: they're Levites. Some families named Levi, Levine, Levy or Halevi carry that tribe in their name.
screen: `A PITCHER AND A BASIN.` → `THEY POUR, THEN SIT DOWN.` → `THE LEVITES.`

segments.voice: Numbers chapter three. God tells Moses that the Levites will be taken instead of every firstborn of Israel, "and the Levites shall be Mine." Back in Egypt, the firstborn had been spared on the night of the plague, and so they belonged to God. Now a whole tribe takes their place. Rashi links the choice to the golden calf: when Moses called out who is on the LORD's side, the tribe of Levi came. Levi's name comes from the story of his birth in Genesis. His mother Leah hoped that now her husband would be joined to her. Levi, joined. And that's the job. Aaron's family within the tribe are the priests, who offer at the altar. The rest of the Levites are joined to them: they guard the Tabernacle, take it down, carry its pieces through the desert, and set it up again. Later, in the Temple, the Bible remembers them as singers and gatekeepers. They get no portion of land like the other tribes; they live in cities scattered among everyone else. Their inheritance, the Torah says elsewhere, is God. In synagogues today, a Levite is customarily called second to the Torah reading, and at the priestly blessing, Levites may wash the priests' hands. And Maimonides widens the door. Not only the tribe of Levi, he writes, but any person whose spirit moves them to stand before God and serve becomes holy. The role is inherited. The calling is open.

434.title: Bamidbar: teachers are parents (Numbers 3:1)
434.hook: Aaron's sons are called Moses' too; whoever teaches a child is like a parent (Sanhedrin 19b)
434.howItsDone: Jewish tradition gives teachers great honor; the Talmud's teaching that whoever teaches another's child Torah is as if they gave birth to them is often quoted at teacher-appreciation events and at the close of a child's studies.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Levites were set apart. Your line was set apart to serve. Today, a family tree that looks wrong.

Almost everyone can name one. The teacher who stayed after class. The coach who saw something in a kid nobody else did. The aunt who taught you to read music, the neighbor who taught you to ride a bike, the camp counselor whose voice you still hear when you're scared. They aren't on your birth certificate. But if someone asked who made you who you are, their names would come up fast. The Torah has a verse that seems, at first, to have made a mistake in a family tree. The rabbis decided it hadn't.
screen: `THE ONE WHO STAYED AFTER CLASS.` → `NOT ON THE BIRTH CERTIFICATE.` → `A FAMILY TREE THAT LOOKS WRONG.`

segments.voice: Numbers three, verse one: "Now these are the generations of Aaron and Moses in the day that the LORD spoke with Moses in mount Sinai." You'd expect two lists of children. Then verse two names the sons, and they're only Aaron's: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. Moses' own sons aren't there. So why is the heading Aaron and Moses? The Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin, page nineteen b, answers in a sentence quoted ever since. Aaron fathered them; Moses taught them. And so Scripture counts them as his. Whoever teaches Torah to someone else's child, the Talmud says, it is as if they had given birth to that child. The same page has a sister teaching. In the book of Samuel, some children are named as Michal's, though another woman bore them. The Talmud explains: Michal raised them, and whoever raises an orphan in their home is counted by Scripture as the parent. Put the two together and you get a wide, generous idea of family. Parenthood is something you do as well as something you are. In Jewish tradition, the teacher holds a near-sacred place, and the old law codes discuss honoring one's teacher alongside honoring one's parents. Rashi, reading this very verse, says it plainly: Moses taught them Torah, so they're called his offspring. A family tree, on this reading, has more branches than the birth records show.
screen: `AARON AND MOSES: ONE LIST.` · `ONLY AARON'S SONS ARE NAMED.` · `WHOEVER TEACHES A CHILD.` · `WHOEVER RAISES AN ORPHAN.` · then, large: `TEACHERS ARE PARENTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Think of a child in your life, your own, a niece, a student, a friend's kid, or the child you once were, and ask who taught that child something that stuck: a teacher, a coach, a babysitter, an older cousin. Picture them, and let yourself feel grateful in a specific way: for this lesson, on that day.
Bamidbar. This week in the wilderness book: still remembered, be strong, the wilderness teaches, count every head, everyone around the center, set apart to serve, and teachers are parents too.
Your line: teachers are parents too. Some of your family never shared your name. See you tomorrow.
